On November 22, 2022, Bhuvneshwar Kumar played his last match for India, against New Zealand. Four years later, he has returned to the Indian T20I squad against the same opposition.The recall came on earlier this week, when the BCCI announced India's squad for the five-match T20I series in New Zealand. The 36-year-old’s name was one of the biggest talking points in the 16-member squad.In between were four years without an India call-up, a shift from international regular to domestic leader, and a fitness routine that, according to the man who has worked closely with him, demanded hours every day.A few months before his return, he had taken 28 wickets in 16 matches for Royal Challengers Bengaluru in IPL 2026, finishing as the joint-highest wicket-taker of the season. His wickets came at an average of 17.89 and an economy rate of 7.95 as RCB won their second successive IPL title.After the IPL, Bhuvneshwar captained Lucknow Falcons in the UPT20 league to the final, taking 14 wickets in 11 matches at 16.57, with an economy rate of 6.82.After RCB made it to their back-to-back final of IPL, TimesofIndia.com spoke to Bhuvneshwar's personal strength and conditioning coach, Surya Pratap Yadav, about the changes behind the scenes. One of the biggest areas of focus was body composition. “Our primary focus has been reducing body fat while increasing muscle mass. As athletes age, muscle loss becomes a concern, so we worked extensively on strength training, protein intake, and supplementation.“Bhuvneshwar's body fat percentage has come down from 19% to 14%, while maintaining his weight, which indicates muscle gain. His strength levels have improved significantly, and that has helped increase force production and running speed,” Surya Pratap had told TimesofIndia.com in May this year.“Discipline is the biggest factor. He understands his body's weak points and works on them proactively. We dedicate nearly an hour every day to rehab and injury-prevention exercises. Along with that, we focus heavily on recovery, hydration, sleep, protein intake, and supplements. All of these factors help him stay fit throughout the season,” added Pratap.“A lot more than people realise, he spends 6-7 hours a day training. That includes gym sessions, rehabilitation work, recovery routines, batting practice, bowling practice, and training in different environments. Even if it isn't always visible on social media, the amount of effort he puts in every day is tremendous,” Surya Pratap Yadav had said.For a fast bowler in his mid-30s, that workload has to be managed as carefully as the bowling itself. Bhuvneshwar's answer was to make the routine part of his cricket life rather than something reserved for a comeback attempt.The years after his India exit were not spent away from competitive cricket. Bhuvneshwar remained a key figure for Uttar Pradesh in domestic cricket, leading the bowling attack in competitions including the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy and Vijay Hazare Trophy. The IPL remained another constant.He had already stopped attaching his daily work to the expectation of a national recall, but the grind continued. In a video posted by RCB, Bhuvneshwar explained why he had stopped setting long-term targets.“I am not thinking about India’s comeback. It has been many years since I stopped keeping or making long-term goals because whenever I did that, it never worked for me. I am happy that I have played 200 matches and taken so many wickets in the powerplay and at the death. I think it is all a reward for what I have done over the years.Bhuvneshwar's return for the NZ series also puts his bowling in a wider context. He has long been one of India's most effective swing bowlers, particularly when the new ball offers movement. His overseas record has included strong spells in England, the West Indies, South Africa and other conditions where the ability to move the ball in the air remains valuable.However, his returns in New Zealand have been modest - having taken 15 wickets in 15 matches, with an average of 38.00. His numbers on the last New Zealand trip: four wickets in five T20Is at an average of 40.00 and an economy rate of 8.42.But the relevance of Bhuvneshwar's return is not confined to the numbers from one series. His new-ball swing gives India another type of option, particularly as the team looks towards conditions in New Zealand.The comeback also attracted attention from former India players. Suresh Raina called the selection ‘thoroughly deserved’, while Kris Srikkanth described it as a ‘fantastic move’. Virender Sehwag questioned whether age should be a deciding factor if a 35- or 36-year-old fast bowler is still producing match-winning performances. Mohammad Kaif has also pointed to Bhuvneshwar's ability to trouble batters with movement.
Article Summary: Bhuvneshwar Kumar has been recalled to India's T20 squad. The 36-year-old has not played for India since November 22, 2022. He has taken 28 wickets in 16 matches for Royal Challengers Bengaluru in IPL 2026.

Article Title: India vs West Indies in Ranchi brings back an Ajit Agarkar memory - but his role has completely changed

NEW DELHI: Ajit Agarkar will not be around the selection table when India take on West Indies in the second T20I at the JSCA International Stadium Complex on Friday. But the former India pacer has an interesting connection with Ranchi and the venue.The last time Ranchi hosted a T20I, Agarkar was there too - not as the chairman of the BCCI selection committee, but as a pitch expert.In 2023, when India played New Zealand in a T20I at the same venue, Agarkar did the pitch report before the match.As part of the broadcast coverage, Agarkar assessed the playing conditions and pointed out the dimensions of the ground, the grass cover and the possible impact of dew."The average first innings score is 156. Square boundaries are little over 60 and straight boundaries are little over 70, in the corner around the players pavilion it's only 57 and 59 metres. The pitch looks excellent, there is even covering of grass and there might be some help with the new ball. There is a lot of talk about the dew, the curator kept the grass as minimum as possible on the outfield to negate the dew factor. The ball will skid on nicely, but looks an excellent pitch for batting," reckon Ajit Agarkar in 2023.Three years later, as India return to Ranchi for another T20I, Agarkar’s tenure as chairman of selectors has come to an end.The BCCI invited applications on Tuesday to fill the vacant position in the men’s selection committee following Agarkar’s exit. Agarkar’s tenure ended on October 4. The former India pacer had informed the board after its Annual General Meeting on September 18 that he would not seek an extension.Pragyan Ojha is currently the interim chairman of selectors, with Shiv Sundar Das, Ajay Ratra and RP Singh the other members of the panel.“The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) invites applications for one position on its Men's Selection Committee," the BCCI said on its website.The deadline for applications is October 14.Agarkar leaves the post after a successful period for Indian cricket. During his tenure, India won the 2024 and 2026 T20 World Cups and the 2025 Champions Trophy. The team also won two Asia Cup titles and back-to-back Asian Games gold medals, while reaching the 2023 ODI World Cup final.His tenure also saw the beginning of a major transition in Indian cricket, with Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma retiring from T20Is and Tests.The BCCI thanked Agarkar for his contribution and highlighted the major achievements during his time as chairman.“A tenure marked by some truly special moments for Indian cricket — three ICC trophies, two Asia Cup titles and back-to-back Asian Games Gold medals, along with a run to the 2023 ODI World Cup final,” the BCCI posted on its official X account.“Thank you, Mr Ajit Agarkar for your commitment, conviction and contribution as Chairman of the Men’s Selection Committee. Wishing you the very best for the journey ahead,” the board added.
Article Summary: Ajit Agarkar’s three-year stint as chairman of selectors ends. India take on West Indies in the second T20I at the JSCA International Stadium Complex in Ranchi on Friday. In 2023, when India played New Zealand in a T20i at the same venue, Agarksar did the pitch report before the match.

Article Title: ‘History that will last forever’: Cristiano Ronaldo pays tribute to Lionel Messi with ‘utmost respect’
Article Text:
Ronaldo pays tribute to Lionel Messi after farewell

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Ronaldo’s message to Lionel Messi after international retirement

Cristiano Ronaldo put aside one of football’s most enduring rivalries to pay tribute to Lionel Messi after the Argentine bid an emotional farewell to international football.Messi, 39, made his final appearance for Argentina on Tuesday, signing off in style as he scored once and created two goals in a 3-0 friendly victory over Benin at Buenos Aires’ Monumental Stadium. More than 85,000 fans were present as Argentina celebrated the end of his remarkable 21-year international career.Following the match, Messi took to Instagram to reflect on his journey with the national team and admitted that he was already missing the feeling of representing Argentina in the famous blue and white shirt."Yesterday was my last game, and I already miss wearing the blue and white. I know I'm making the right decision," Messi said in a lengthy Instagram post. "It's been an incredible journey, full of joy and also some sadness, but I know for sure that every step I took was worth it..."I don't want to forget Diego (Maradona), who put our country where it deserved to be and who, as I always say, I know helped us both by being here with us and also from heaven, with every step we took."Thank you to the clubs where I played, for always respecting my feelings and allowing me to dedicate myself to my country whenever it was time to put on the national team jersey..."Messi's international career included Argentina's 2022 World Cup triumph, Copa America titles in 2021 and 2024, and victory in the 2022 Finalissima."I am grateful. I love you all very much; I'm going to miss you, and I will always thank you for having been by our side, by my side," the Inter Miami playmaker added.Among those to respond to Messi's farewell message was Ronaldo, his long-time rival in the debate over the greatest player of their generation. Despite their careers being defined by competition for individual and team honours, the Portugal captain offered a warm tribute to the Argentine."Leo, after so many years of defending your country, you've made history that will last forever. I have the utmost respect for what you've accomplished with Argentina. A hug," Ronaldo said.Ronaldo, 41, has himself been in the spotlight with Portugal after becoming embroiled in a dispute with coach Jorge Jesus following his abrupt departure from the national team's training camp.For Messi, however, the international chapter ended with a memorable night in front of a packed Monumental, bringing an emotional close to more than two decades of representing Argentina.
Article Summary: Cristiano Ronaldo pays tribute to Lionel Messi after his international retirement. Messi made his final appearance for Argentina in a 3-0 friendly victory over Benin. The 39-year-old scored once and created two goals in Buenos Aires' Monumental Stadium.

Article Title: ‘Play more cricket’: Kapil Dev’s blunt take on Hardik Pandya’s injury woes
Article Text:
Hardik Pandya (AFP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view What is the biggest factor contributing to player injuries in cricket? High volume of cricket Lack of training Inadequate rest Player fitness levels 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Hardik Pandya’s prolonged absence from competitive cricket has once again brought the issue of player workload, game time and injuries into focus, with India also dealing with fitness concerns involving several other players.Pandya has not played competitive cricket since the final week of IPL 2026. He was expected to return for India A in the upcoming ODI series against Australia A, beginning October 6, but his comeback was delayed. He is now ruled out of the upcoming white-ball tour of New Zealand.So what does Pandya need to do to be available more often?“Play more cricket,” former India captain Kapil Dev told Times of India.Asked if he felt Pandya was not doing that, Kapil said: “I don’t know. You play more, your body gets tuned to that. But if you play less and suddenly you play more, chances of injury increase. If your muscles are fine, your injuries are less.”Kapil’s comments come at a time when India are dealing with a number of injury concerns. Prasidh Krishna has been ruled out for at least three weeks and is highly likely to miss the upcoming five-match ODI series against New Zealand. India’s tour of New Zealand begins with the T20I series on October 22.Harshit Rana has also suffered a fitness setback and is unlikely to be picked for India’s upcoming tour of New Zealand. Rana was ruled out of the three-match T20I series against Afghanistan as well as the 2026 Asian Games last month due to injury. He was recovering at the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru but developed low-grade pain in his left quadriceps during a match simulation.Pandya, meanwhile, has been away from competitive cricket since the conclusion of IPL 2026, while Harshit last featured during India’s white-ball leg against England in July.The wider spread of cricket injuries over the last four-five years also prompted a discussion with Kapil on whether the volume of cricket has contributed to the problem.The former India captain pointed to the difference in the playing patterns of his generation, citing Sandeep Patil’s observation about how players used to remain involved in different forms of domestic cricket.“Sandeep Patil put it very nicely. ‘In our time we used to play Ranji Trophy , Duleep Trophy, club cricket, other cricket too.’ In 365 days, if you can play 250 days, you’re in the game.”For Kapil, regular cricket helps the body stay accustomed to the demands of the game. For India, Pandya’s prolonged absence and the fitness concerns surrounding several other players underline the challenge of keeping key players available for longer stretches.
Article Summary: Hardik Pandya has not played competitive cricket since the final week of IPL 2026. He was expected to return for India A in the upcoming ODI series against Australia A, beginning October 6, but his comeback was delayed. He is now ruled out of the upcoming white-ball tour of New Zealand. Former India captain Kapil Dev says Pandya needs to play more cricket.

Article Title: Red to pink ball? MCC official clarifies how ICC’s new Test trial will work
Article Text:
ICC allows pink ball usage

Modern cricket is batter-friendly, and now the ICC playing conditions say five penalty runs for time-wasting. Is it a way of levelling the playing field?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

On pink-ball trial in day-time Tests...

One big concern is the over rates. How does MCC act on this?

Bengaluru: With the game of cricket constantly evolving, the International Cricket Council (ICC) made a slew of changes to its playing conditions, which came into effect from Oct 1. Some of those changes included a pink-ball trial in Tests and time-wasting penalties.Fraser Stewart, the Head of Cricket at Marylebone Cricket Club, opened up beyond the laws in a media interaction here on Monday.The law has always been there. It’s just rarely been enacted, and I think now the ICC have said, right, we’re going to try to toughen up on this a bit. I think the more we can do to try to speed up play, the better it is. Otherwise, the public who pay a lot of money to watch cricket feel short-changed.I think what the umpires try to do is to highlight to players that there are laws that cover this and if you waste time, it will catch up and there will be an in-game penalty of runs rather than a fine afterwards.That’s an ICC playing condition rather than a law of cricket. I believe, in a bilateral series, say, India playing Australia, it’s for them to agree among themselves for a particular game, are we going to use a pink ball?Some people have thought you can start with a red ball and then when it gets a bit dark, you switch to pink.That’s not, as I understand it, what’s happening. Both need to agree and if they are happy to play with the pink ball, perhaps because they think that it’ll mean there can be more play after bad weather.The laws do provide a remedy, both for batting and bowling sides. It’s for umpires to enforce those laws and, if they think the pace of play is too slow, whether it is the fielding captain or the batting side, and say, you’re on a warning; it will result in penalty runs.But the umpires do need to enforce that, and be backed up by the match referees.
Article Summary: The International Cricket Council (ICC) made a slew of changes to its playing conditions, which came into effect from Oct 1. Some of those changes included a pink-ball trial in Tests and time-wasting penalties. Fraser Stewart, the Head of Cricket at Marylebone Cricket Club, opened up beyond the laws.

Article Title: Khalid Jamil’s bolder India faces Uruguay as Forlan begins rebuilding after World Cup debacle
Article Text:

KOLKATA: In the past few days, Diego Forlan and his Uruguay team have been staying here like passive guests, happily blending into the background and letting Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil enjoy the public eye. With the departure of their fellow South American rivals, the spotlight is back on La Celeste. So is India’s final act of their extraordinary brush with three World Cup teams in this Fifa international window.Being a football team in transition comes with its own set of challenges. In holding Panama 1-1 and even in losing 0-4 to Brazil, Khalid Jamil’s team has shown glimpses of promise. Teams under Jamil are always known for being defensively strong; sitting deep in numbers is a celebrated way of making life difficult for the opponents. A paradigm shift is now noticeable in the system. India look bolder, more ambitious.“It’s not about me and all credit goes to players,” the former India midfielder told TOI during the pre-match news conference on Monday, the eve of their clash with Uruguay at Salt Lake Stadium.Jamil, however, has warned his players of not repeating the mistakes they had committed against Brazil. “Don’t concede early,” was his advice.Uruguay have stars like Darwin Nunez, Rodrigo Bentancur, Ronald Araujo and Jose Maria in their squad with players equipped with elite mentality. Ranked 20th in the world, they are expected to come hard at the home team with their typical aggression and physicality.Forlan, Golden Ball winner of the 2010 World Cup and an icon in Uruguayan football, also is tasked with rebuilding a team whose World Cup campaigned collapsed into a player revolt against his predecessor Marcelo Bielsa.“I want my players to understand that I’m going to be the same if they win and I’m going to be the same if they lose. But the most important thing is to give your best,” Forlan said in replying to a question from the TOI.“When you win, you’re not the best and when you lose you’re not the worst,” he said.
Article Summary: India take on Uruguay in their final World Cup warm-up match. Khalid Jamil's team have shown glimpses of promise in recent matches. Uruguay have stars like Darwin Nunez, Rodrigo Bentancur, Ronald Araujo and Jose Maria.

Article Title: India 'A' pacers look to step up to the plate against Australia 'A'
Article Text:

PUDUCHERRY: In an era where 350-plus totals in ODIs are becoming the norm, fast bowlers are often left walking a tightrope. India’s recent ODI series against the West Indies was a case in point, with the bowlers conceding 295 and 405 in the first two games before West Indies chased down 352 in the final ODI with 10 balls to spare.As India look towards the 2027 World Cup, where they begin their campaign against Australia on Oct 7, the threematch one-day series between India ‘A’ and Australia ‘A’ in Puducherry offers another window into the country’s pace reserves.The big question is: who can eventually emerge as the ideal partner for Jasprit Bumrah With Arshad Khan , Gurjapneet Singh and Yash Thakur are part of the India ‘A’ setup, it will be interesting to see if anyone can step up.India ‘A’ coach Lakshmipathy Balaji believes the cupboard is far from bare. For him, the answer lies as much in patience and nurturing as it does in raw numbers.“Many have potential. High-scoring games are common now, but bowlers will adapt over time. Bumrah became world-class through time, effort and experience. Youngsters like Anshul (Kamboj) and Gurnoor (Brar) need time and grooming to match international demands. It won’t always be 350-400 run games; bowlers will adapt to modern demands very soon,” Balaji said.Anshul Kamboj was handed his ODI debut in the third game against West Indies after Prasidh Krishna was ruled out. It was, however, a baptism of fire as he conceded 82 runs in nine overs. Gurnoor Brar, who has nine ODIs under his belt, also had an expensive series, while Auqib Nabi went for 84 in 8.5 overs on his ODI debut. Prasidh, too, had a difficult outing in his two games.Yet Balaji does not see the recent run-fests as a cause for concern.“Nothing is lacking, everyone is working hard. Since both teams have scored heavily, batting has temporarily moved ahead of bowling in modern cricket. Once bowling units click together, a balanced contest between bat and ball will return soon,” he said.
Article Summary: India 'A' coach Lakshmipathy Balaji says bowlers will adapt to modern demands. Balaji believes bowlers need time and grooming to match international demands. India begin their 2027 World Cup campaign against Australia on Oct 7 in Puducherry.

Article Title: ‘Greatest pile of mediocrity’: Matthew Hayden tears into Australia selectors over ‘disrespecting first-class cricket’
Article Text:
Matthew Hayden (Getty Images)

Hayden questions alternative options

Former Australia opener Matthew Hayden has launched a strong criticism of the national selection panel over Nic Maddinson’s recall for the three-Test series against South Africa, questioning the decision to bring back a batter who has not played first-class cricket since early 2025.Maddinson, 34, was added to Australia’s squad amid a mounting injury crisis ahead of the series opener in Durban on October 9. Josh Inglis has been ruled out with a finger injury, while Cameron Green remains a doubt for the first Test.However, Hayden believes the circumstances do not justify Maddinson’s return to the Test set-up, particularly given his lack of recent first-class cricket.Speaking on the All Over Bar The Cricket podcast, the former 103-Test opener questioned whether Maddinson would be capable of making a significant impact if Australia called upon him during the series.“Where we are at is that we are promoting the greatest pile of mediocrity that we’ve seen in a generation of cricket,” Hayden said on the All Over Bar The Cricket podcast.Hayden also took aim at chief selector George Bailey and Tony Dodemaide, arguing that Australia should be selecting players with stronger first-class records rather than relying on batters with modest averages.“And if we continue to lay that out and expect that a bloke averaging 35 is going to average 55 in Test match cricket, George Bailey and Tony Dodemaide, you are dreaming.I will just put it that simply. You are frigging dreaming. And you are piling up this dog s*** explanation, and you are, in my opinion, disrespecting first-class cricket. Absolutely dead set you are. You should be picking guys that are averaging 45 or more, and you can’t, because they don’t want to play," said Hayden.Maddinson has not featured in a Test since the 2016-17 home summer, when he scored just 27 runs across three matches. His first-class average of 37.11 has further fuelled the debate around his selection.His return to the squad comes after a difficult period that included treatment for testicular cancer.Hayden suggested Sam Harper could have been considered instead. The wicketkeeper-batter recently impressed on Australia A’s tour of India, where he also scored a century, before being added to the Test squad.The former opener also questioned the selection credentials of all-rounder Mitchell Marsh, pointing to his limited participation in state-level red-ball cricket.Hayden argued that Marsh’s lack of Shield cricket should matter despite Australia captain Pat Cummins backing the all-rounder.“I don’t care what Pat Cummins said about Mitch – if he doesn’t want to play Shield cricket … it’s a desire to front up,” Hayden said.He further criticised the growing preference among players for franchise cricket over domestic red-ball cricket, identifying it as a wider issue for Australian cricket.“They don’t want to play this version of the game. Mitch is a good example. He is making millions of dollars playing cricket all over the world for franchises. This is the fundamental problem we have," added Hayden.
Article Summary: Nic Maddinson has not played first-class cricket since early 2025. The 34-year- old has not featured in a Test since the 2016-17 home summer, when he scored just 27 runs across three matches. Hayden believes the circumstances do not justify Maddinson’s return to the Test set-up, particularly given his lack of recent first class cricket.

NEW DELHI: Savitha Shri Baskar emerged as India's golden girl at the 2026 Chess Olympiad, but there was a point when her chess career was funded by her father's gold jewellery, pawned to cover a national tournament's entry fee.Baskar, an electrician in Singapore at the time, would go on to quit that job entirely and move back to India to support her daughter. It was a decision he still calls difficult.The sacrifice, in fact, wasn't only his to make. Chess had first entered the family through Savitha's older brother Mugesh, whom their father had originally set out to build a career around.Savitha's own interest came from watching him play. But once both children were training together, the costs made running two chess careers impossible. Mugesh stepped back after the eighth standard. Savitha kept going.This time, she went to Samarkand as the youngest member of the Indian contingent, brought in after Harika Dronavalli, who felt she'd achieved everything a chess career could offer , including a gold, stepped aside for the next generation.Even then, there were questions about the 19-year-old International Master's spot in the squad. "There were a lot of people who questioned her spot, journalists saying there are players higher than her, and so on," women's captain Swayams Mishra had earlier told TimesofIndia.com "But according to the selection, she was qualified, and she'd won the Asian continental a couple of months ago. She'd also played the World Women's Team Championship, so I knew her as a team player always. Whenever we gave her the opportunity, she delivered. If India won a medal, we owe it to her."Savitha delivered in some style, becoming the only Indian to win an individual gold medal in Uzbekistan, finishing an extraordinary 9/10, and a central figure in India's bronze-medal campaign."Coming to the team as a reserve player, I wasn't even expecting to play all 10 rounds," she told TimesofIndia.com during an exclusive interaction. "So I'm grateful for the trust my teammates and my captain had in me, for giving me the opportunity to play all 10. I'm happy with the score, 9 out of 10; but game-wise, I think I could have done a bit better."Around her sat some of the biggest names in Indian women's chess. Looking back at her first experience of the Olympiad, she continued, "It was my first Olympiad, and it has always been a dream for me to play for the country in a tournament like this. We had Humpy (Koneru) akka, who's been the top-most player in women's chess for almost two decades, and we had Vaishali akka and Divya Deshmukh; such a strong team, and we were the first seed in the women's section. I learned a lot from all of them, and Abhijit sir and Swayams sir did a wonderful job with our openings and in every other aspect too. It was a wonderful experience."Despite the individual gold, she's unambiguous about where her priorities sat throughout. "The team medal will always come first, because we're giving out everything for the team. I wasn't even caring about my individual gold; someone told me I'd already secured a medal before the last round, but I only found out I'd won gold after the round finished," she recalled with a laugh. "I was just trying my best to win that last game so we could get a silver as a team. From the position I got, I couldn't really convert anything, but I'm at least happy we got the bronze."The campaign didn't begin smoothly off the board. "When we arrived (in Samarkand) at the hotel, it was around 11:30 at night, and they said they couldn't get the rooms ready," Savitha told this website. "We didn't get our rooms for five or six hours. They made us wait in the lobby, then gave one or two rooms for the whole team."What followed, though, was a federation stepping up as Savitha confirmed, "After that, AICF made sure everything was sorted, and that we got our Indian food every day. The Indian restaurant was so far away that they had to arrange someone to get the delivery done, and they made sure the food was good quality and on time. I don't think any federation would have done that. We're all so grateful for it."On the board, the campaign's defining stretch came against Kazakhstan and China, the two matches where her own result decided India's fate."With both teams, I was the one playing till the last point, and my game was going to be the deciding factor," she said. "It started with Kazakhstan; I got an equal position and was trying to push it. I think what helped me score was time management: after move 40 I was always ahead on the clock compared to my opponent, which put more pressure on them, and I was able to swindle the position."Against China, the margins were just as tight. "It's a bit sad we couldn't win that one," the teenager added. "When I got a better position, Vantika made a blunder at that point and got into a worse position. If she'd been able to hold a draw, I think we'd have got gold fairly easily."Through the toughest stretches, Savitha points to one figure in particular for keeping the team together, especially after an early loss to Poland."Swayams sir is the best captain ever, I think, because of the way he handled our team. We lost to Poland, but he was the one who motivated us. Even during games, if we wanted something, he was always there: water, bananas, everything. For me, he was bringing endless coffees, because I played till the last moment every time. He even jokingly said it was because of those coffees that I was able to swing all my games." The backing went beyond logistics, she said. "He had so much confidence in me. I think he believed in me more than I believed in myself."That trust, she added, was something she'd first experienced a cycle earlier, at the Asian Games, and carried with her into Samarkand."There's just so much you learn from being in a team like that, discussing lines together in team meetings, having those interactions, and them having so much confidence in me. They believed in me more than I did in myself at the time too," she noted.Asked whether she thinks back to what her family gave up to get her here, Savitha is candid, albeit guarded, about letting it weigh on her day-to-day. "If I don't play well, it all comes back to mind. My parents struggled. I know what they've gone through, because they had to spend so much on chess because of me. That's something I'll always remember. But I don't really think much about it while I'm playing, or in general. I just have to stay in the present.Savitha, currently rated 2405, is treating the grandmaster (GM) title as a goal to work toward rather than something owed to her on reputation."The Grandmaster title is definitely my goal, and I'll be working towards it," she said in a confident voice. "I'll be playing tournaments, of course, but for now I think I'll take a bit of rest. The Olympiad is such a big and tiring event. My next tournament will probably be the World Juniors in Namibia, though I might play something before that. I haven't decided yet."On where her game itself needs to sharpen next, she concluded, "In my own game, I think I should get a bit steadier in the openings, and probably work on some positional stuff as well. In the Olympiad, I played the aggressive, complicated positions pretty well; positional chess is the other part I'll be working on."
Article Summary: Savitha Shri Baskar is the only Indian to win an individual gold medal in Uzbekistan. She was brought in after Harika Dronavalli, who felt she'd achieved everything a chess career could offer, stepped aside for the next generation. The 19-year-old International Master was a central figure in India's bronze- medal campaign.

Article Title: ‘We’re not trying to be any other league’: SA20 COO Lynn Naudé on the league’s rapid rise
Article Text:
Lynn Naudé (left), COO of SA20 (Special Arrangement)

Excerpts

SA20 has grown rapidly in four seasons. What has been the biggest lesson behind that success?

How do you keep SA20 distinct in an increasingly crowded global T20 calendar?

What role has the league played in strengthening South African cricket beyond the professional level?

With overseas leagues expanding, how do you ensure SA20 continues attracting elite international players?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Looking ahead to Season 5, what is the one area where you want fans to notice a clear step forward?

NEW DELHI: Four seasons into its existence, SA20 has already established itself as one of the most prominent T20 leagues outside the IPL. But for COO Lynn Naudé, the league’s rapid rise has been less about chasing quick wins and more about getting the fundamentals right. From securing a prime South African summer window and putting Proteas at the heart of the competition to creating a strong match-day atmosphere, Naudé explains how SA20 has built its identity and what lies ahead in Season 5.I think probably the biggest lesson is that strong foundations matter more than quick wins. From the very start, we were very single-minded about what we believed success looked like. The fan experience, the quality of cricket and putting South African players at the heart of the competition were all important to us. We wanted to make sure SA20 felt like it belonged to South African fans as a starting point, and then we could take it global from there.I think that's probably been one of my biggest learnings. If you can get your basics right, the rest will follow from thereT20 cricket has got a unique feeling to it, and that's possibly a common thread. But I think there are a couple of things that have helped us.First, our window and our ability to secure it in the heart of the South African summer, with great conditions and full stadiums, was a real coup for us.That time of year lends itself to delivering a product that speaks very much to the fans, but also provides a fantastic experience both on broadcast and in the stadium.The second is the quality of the competition. The commitment from Cricket South Africa to make all of its Proteas available to play in the tournament season after season, and to see them compete with the best in the world, means that we have intentionally put cricket at the heart of the product.The third is probably the atmosphere at the venues. I think that's become something quite synonymous with SA20.If I had to wrap it up, I'd say we're not trying to be any other league. We're just trying to be the best version of SA20 that we can be.”It has actually been on multiple levels. The intention was for SA20 to almost become a bastion for South African cricket. There was obviously work that needed to be done to strengthen the talent pipeline.But outside of that, if I look back again on the last five seasons, it's also about the quality of the broadcast, what's improved in terms of the fan experience within the South African sporting context, our venues, the ways of working and how they operate on a day-to-day basis.There's also been a lot of knowledge transfer from SA20 into the greater cricket ecosystem, with some of the standards and expectations that we have for the type of product we want to deliver.We've had the opportunity to expose a lot of young talent in the sporting industry to our ways of working and the culture at SA20.In the lead-up to the 2027 World Cup, what we've tried to do is make sure that the cricket ecosystem, and those who deliver not only on the field but also off it, is better off the back of SA20 and the experience it has brought to the South African cricket landscape.At the highest level, elite players want to play where the cricket is competitive, the conditions are good and the environment is professional. I think that's something we strive to offer, and I think we do offer all three.Our franchises bring global experience and know how to run teams. The players know that when they come here, they'll be tested against strong domestic talent and they'll be playing in front of full stadiums.It's always surprising to me, anecdotally, when I hear players talk about how important it is to them to play in front of a crowd and how different it feels. I guess when you're talented like that, you feel appreciated when you're playing in front of a lot of people.That, coupled with the strong and stable franchise ownership groups that we've got, who invest in those players, offers them opportunities.If you have the opportunity to play in the SA20, you also have the opportunity to play in many other places around the world. I think consistency across all of those things will make sure that we remain attractive to players.Every season we run a fan survey, and it directly shapes what we deliver. Our fans have told us what they want to see more of, and they've also told us what they don't want us to change. Those are the types of things that shape our decisions.Our brand positioning at SA20 is ‘for everyone’, and we take that pretty seriously. On the field, it means competitive, world-class cricket for the dedicated cricket fan. Off the field, it really means a great social occasion for people to come and enjoy the atmosphere, the music and a day out with friends and family.If I have to say what I want fans to take away, it's that we do hear you, we do listen to what you want, and we will always strive to deliver based on the feedback that fans are giving us.
Article Summary: Lynn Naudé, COO of SA20, talks to TOI about the league's rapid rise. SA20 has established itself as one of the most prominent T20 leagues outside the IPL. COO says league's success has been down to getting the fundamentals right. He talks about securing a prime South African summer window.

Greater Noida: Brand Kapil Dev was a thing much before brand was anything in Indian sports. His was a truly organic, everlasting phenomenon. Today, it is being put to use in perhaps just the way it was always meant to be — playing it forward.As president of the Professional Golf Tour of India (PGTI), a role he has slipped into like the proverbial glove, the former India Test captain and 1983 World Cup winner is helping add huge value to Indian golf.On Wednesday, shadows lengthening at the Jaypee Greens Golf & Spa Resort course, Kapil sat on the clubhouse green, gazing benignly at the last of the groups putting home in a tournament named after him. Excerpts...They’ve done it without my knowing it. They contacted my office and it was decided. It should be a President Cup, not Kapil Dev Invitational. I am just a worker.No, no. You can’t say coach. If I give you a job for 10 days, you can’t become a coach.I was not working even six months (as coach). I wouldn’t consider that a coaching assignment.I feel very happy. If we can do something for golf. I love to do work for cricket but if they don’t invite me, I have to do something. So I feel very happy to do it for golf.Had I played golf then, it would have helped with concentration. One bad shot can get you out in cricket too, but here your target is small.Just go and enjoy yourself. Cricketers should understand they are playing for pleasure and making the game more popular. If they want to be a professional then they have to have a different frame of mind.You need eight to 10 hours (daily) workload. Golf is very, very tough.I don’t think I can judge. Only those who are playing can.Play more cricket.I don’t know. You play more, your body gets tuned to that. But if you play less and suddenly you play more, chances of injury increase. If your muscles are fine, your injuries are less.Sandeep Patil put it very nicely. ‘In our time we used to play Ranji Trophy , Duleep Trophy, club cricket, other cricket too.’ In 365 days, if you can play 250 days, you’re in the game.I don’t watch cricket. Yes, if I see the highlights or something special happens, you definitely go and see and enjoy that.A little bit of equipment. The bats have changed. These young boys are very confident, much better. They get a lot more opportunities. In our time, if you’re out of the team, you have to play Ranji Trophy, Duleep Trophy. The opportunities these cricketers have is a lot.The board has given them more opportunities to come back and perform, like Bhuvi (Bhuvneshwar Kumar). He’s come back after four years because he played in the IPL, performed and bounced back. But here, more credit to Bhuvi than anybody else. Because in a cricketing sense, they really write you off very fast. But he kept on working with the opportunities that he got.If you don’t give the golfers infrastructure, how will they improve? All top golfers, they still can’t walk in to play in any golf course. Give them a better place to practise and play. Then it’s a different thing altogether.Today, if you tell a top golfer to go play, they have to pay wherever they have to play, even at this course. As administrators, we feel very sorry for this limitation. The top 40 or 50 pros in this country should be able to walk in to play at any of the golf courses.Any young cricketer who we can feel has a future for the next 10 years, 15 years. Those type of cricketers. We have seen Rohit, Virat. We already saw Sachin. And they made us so proud. (But) you’re always looking for the next hero. You always ask, ‘Who is the next hero?’As a cricketer I like to see which is that young boy who has got that chance, who can replace Virat Kohli. And play for 15 years. That’s what my mind looks for.It’s too early. Does he have the ability? Yes. But there have been so many in cricket who came with so much ability, then faded out.Look at Vinod Kambli. What will we say about that? Vaibhav is 16 years old. Give him another three years, then we will talk. When his lifestyle changes, his thinking too will change. Then we’ll come to know how he will look after the next two years. That is more important than looking at his performance.He’s fabulous. Hats off to him. With that action, he’s proved people like us wrong. We never thought he could survive with that action and bowl so well and become world leading bowler. Tremendous.Everybody can help him, only if he helps himself. I don’t believe in giving him money. I would rather pay his hospital expenses or rehab expenses. Why has he reached this situation? Kambli has himself to blame.As cricketers, we’ve done it twice already. That’s their government, their policy. I’d like to see that they should look after him properly, on a humanitarian basis. He was a great cricketer... five, six years senior to me. We grew up watching him play. I admire him.

Article Title: ‘I’m not going to the military’: What is military exemption? Why South Korea weighs cuts after Asian Games backlash
Article Text:
South Korean football team after winning the Asian Games gold medal. (Pic credit: X)

What is South Korea's military exemption for athletes?

Why is South Korea considering cuts now?

History of the athlete exemption

Who else benefited at the Asian Games?

Will South Korea abolish military exemptions for athletes?

South Korea is reconsidering a decades-old military service benefit for elite athletes after controversial comments by Asian Games gold medallists triggered a fresh public debate over whether sporting success should continue to qualify some young men for an alternative to the country's compulsory military service.The controversy erupted after South Korea won the men's football gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, beating Japan 1-0 in the final on Saturday. Several players came under fire for comments and social-media activity related to the military benefit that came with their gold medal.Captain Lee Gi-hyuk, winger Yang Min-hyuk and forward Park Seung-soo all faced criticism. Lee held up his gold medal and said, “I’m not going to the military,” while Yang said the military-service benefit had been his main motivation during the tournament. Park posted a photograph of himself wearing a cap associated with people who have completed their mandatory military service.All three subsequently apologised. But the episode reignited a much bigger question in South Korea: why should athletes receive special treatment when most young men are required to serve?The government is now reviewing the system.Culture, Sports and Tourism Minister Chae Hwi-young said Wednesday that his ministry would consult the sports and arts communities, the Defence Ministry and the Military Manpower Administration as it considers comprehensive measures.The Defence Ministry has gone further. It said it was considering either scaling back or abolishing supplementary military service for artists and athletes, while Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul said the ministry's goal was to gradually reduce the exemptions and ultimately abolish them.South Korea has a mandatory military-service system under which able-bodied men generally have to complete between 18 and 21 months of service.But athletes who achieve specified international sporting results can receive an alternative-service benefit instead of serving the standard term. Under the current rules, athletes who win an Olympic medal or an Asian Games gold medal qualify for the arrangement.The term “military exemption” is widely used, but it can be slightly misleading.The athletes are not simply released from every military-related obligation. Those who qualify are assigned to supplementary service. They undergo three weeks of basic military training and then have to complete 544 hours of community service over 34 months.For elite athletes, however, the difference is significant.Instead of spending 18 to 21 months in regular military service, they can continue training and competing while completing their alternative-service obligations. That can be particularly important for footballers, golfers, baseball players and other professionals whose careers can be affected by a long interruption during their peak years.The benefit can also have implications for athletes playing overseas because avoiding a lengthy interruption can allow them to maintain their club careers and development.At the 2026 Asian Games, 20 of South Korea's 23 men's football players became eligible for the benefit after the 1-0 victory over Japan.The immediate trigger is the backlash over the footballers' comments.Yang Min-hyuk was criticised after saying the medal and championship were not important to him and that he had played with the military-service benefit in mind.Lee's “I’m not going to the military” remark also drew criticism, while Park's photograph wearing a military discharge-style cap became another focus of the controversy.The players later apologised, with Lee saying he should have considered the weight of his words and Yang explaining that the military benefit was one of several motivations that had been expressed poorly.But the government response suggests the controversy is being viewed as part of a wider problem rather than as an isolated incident.The Defence Ministry said it would consider fairness among people subject to mandatory service, the declining number of people available for military service and public consensus when deciding the future of the supplementary-service system.South Korea's declining birth rate means the pool of young men available for military service is shrinking. That demographic pressure has added importance to the question of who can receive alternative arrangements.There is also a fairness argument. While athletes can qualify through sporting achievements, other high-profile South Koreans have had to complete military service.The issue has been particularly sensitive in the entertainment industry because members of BTS, one of South Korea's biggest cultural exports, completed their military obligations rather than receiving an athlete-style exemption.The comparison has repeatedly featured in the debate over whether exceptional achievements in sport, popular culture or other fields should qualify someone for special treatment.The system dates back to 1973, when South Korea introduced the special arrangement for athletes and artists as part of a broader effort to develop elite talent and enhance the country's international standing.Over the decades, the policy became particularly important in sports such as football and baseball, where military service could interrupt the careers of players competing at home and overseas.The Asian Games has traditionally been especially significant because gold, rather than simply any medal, is required for athletes to qualify.That has sometimes produced unusual incentives around the tournament. For South Korea's football and baseball players, an Asian Games gold medal can effectively remove the possibility of a lengthy interruption to their professional careers.The policy has also generated controversy before.Debates intensified after South Korea's run to the 2002 World Cup semi-finals led to a special exemption arrangement for members of that squad, although the World Cup was later removed from the exemption rules.The system has continued to face questions over whether sporting achievement should be sufficient grounds for an alternative to compulsory service.The football players were not the only South Koreans to qualify.South Korea's baseball players earned the benefit after defeating Japan 3-1 in the final. Gold medallists in esports also qualified under the rules.Golfer Tom Kim won the men's individual gold after travelling to Japan following the Presidents Cup. His response to the military-service issue was markedly different from the comments that triggered the controversy.“I’m more proud that I’m able to bring a medal for my country,” Kim said.The episode therefore illustrates the two sides of the current debate: the argument that sporting success can justify an alternative service arrangement for athletes representing South Korea, and the growing concern that such benefits may be difficult to reconcile with the principle that military service should be shared fairly.There is no immediate abolition, but the government is now openly discussing major changes.The Defence Ministry said it plans to reflect a reduction or abolition of supplementary service for artists and athletes in its defence-reform plans. Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul subsequently said the ministry's goal was to gradually scale back the system and ultimately abolish it.The Culture Ministry is separately reviewing the system and plans to consult athletes, artists, defence officials and the Military Manpower Administration before deciding on comprehensive measures.That means the controversy surrounding the Asian Games footballers could have consequences well beyond their apologies.A system that has existed for more than five decades is now facing a renewed examination at a time when South Korea is dealing with a shrinking pool of young men available for military service and changing public expectations about fairness.For athletes, the debate is ultimately about more than a medal. An Asian Games gold can currently mean the difference between an 18-to-21-month interruption and a much less disruptive alternative-service arrangement.For the government, the question is whether that distinction remains justified — and whether a benefit created more than 50 years ago still fits the realities of modern South Korea.
Article Summary: South Korea is reconsidering a decades-old military service benefit for elite athletes. Controversy erupted after South Korea won the men's football gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, beating Japan 1-0 in the final on Saturday. Several players came under fire for comments and social-media activity related to the military benefit.

NEW DELHI: After a successful Asian Games campaign in Aichi-Nagoya, where India finished fourth in the medal tally with 85 medals, including 21 gold, the country's para-athletes will look to carry the momentum into the Asian Para Games.Paralympic champions Pramod Bhagat and Bhavina Patel have been chosen as India's flag bearers for the Opening Ceremony of the Asian Para Games, scheduled to be held from October 18 to 24 in Nagoya, Japan.Bhagat, one of India's most decorated para badminton players, has won six Asian Para Games medals between 2014 and 2023, including two gold and four bronze. I am excited to walk into the Opening Ceremony with Pramod and lead our contingent.I hope all our athletes compete with confidence, enjoy the moment and give their very best for India.”The Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) will formally send off the Indian contingent at a special ceremony on October 8. Sports Minister Dr Mansukh Mandaviya will attend as chief guest, with Minister of State for Youth Affairs and Sports Raksha Nikhil Khadse as the Guest of Honour.PCI president Devendra Jhajharia said Bhagat and Patel's achievements and resilience made them ideal choices to lead India at the continental para-sport showpiece.“It is a matter of immense pride for us to have Pramod Bhagat and Bhavina Patel lead the Indian contingent at the Opening Ceremony,” Jhajharia said.“Both are exceptional champions who have contributed immensely to the growth of Indian para sport. India’s 21-gold campaign at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games has thrown up an interesting set of numbers: champions who reached the continental podium despite receiving relatively modest targeted financial assistance under the govt’s elite-athlete programmes.Their stories do not diminish the broader support extended to Indian sport. Instead, they underline how performances can sometimes run ahead of the funding pipelines designed to identify and back medal prospects.The clearest example is 17-year-old archer Kumkum Mohod. A recently-inducted Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS) athlete for the Aich-Nagoya preparatory cycle, Kumkum became the first Indian woman to win an individual recurve gold at the Games, defeating South Korea’s Oh Yejin 6-5 after a shoot-off. She also won gold in the women’s recurve team event and silver in mixed team, ending the campaign with three medals and securing India an LA Olympics quota.The funding support extended to her puts her targeted assistance at just Rs 50,000. That is a striking figure against the scale of her achievement, even though her preparation also benefited from the budget allocated to the respective national sports federations (NSFs) under the Annual Calendar for Training and Competition (ACTC).The same pattern is visible in compound archery. Sahil Rajesh Jadhav, who helped India win mixed team gold with Chikitha Taniparthi and also contributed to the men’s team gold, received Rs 50,000 under TOPS during the Games cycle. His top podium finish also delivered India an Olympic quota in compound archery.Kushal Dalal and Thirumuru Ganesh Maniratnam, members of India’s men’s compound team that defeated China for gold, also received only Rs 50,000 each under TOPS during the cycle. Yet the trio of Dalal, Ganesh and Jadhav produced one of India’s five archery gold medals at the Games.The contrast becomes sharper when placed alongside athletes receiving substantially larger targeted allocations. Boxer Ankush Panghal, for instance, received Rs 75,000 under TOPS, while his other gold partners in boxing Lovlina Borgohain and Parveen Hooda received Rs 22.97 lakh and Rs 8.59 lakh assistance, respectively, during the Games cycle.These figures show that support was available at markedly different levels depending on an athlete’s classification, requirements, and timing within the system.Similarly, in sailing, Harshita Tomar and Shital Verma secured the bronze medal in the women’s skiff, with both athletes not being part of the TOPS programme. Also, in the same sport, sailors Manu Francis and Prince Noble won silver in the men’s skiff, but both were not part of either TOPS Core or Development group. Boxer Kapil Pokhariya, too, wasn't part of the TOPS.In shooting, the trio of Manisha Keer, Neeru Dhanda and Aashima Ahlawat won the silver medal in Trap women's team event, with Manisha receiving no TOPS assistance while Neeru, a TOPS Development athlete, getting Rs one lakh. In athletics, silver-wining javelin thrower Yashvir Singh wasn't part of the TOPS funding and largely prepared through the ACTC budget. In kurash, bronze-winner Pincky Balhara, competing in the -78 kg event, received Rs 75,000 under the TAGG scheme during the Games cycle.Kumkum Mohod (Rs 50,000), Sahil Jadhav (Rs 50,000), Kushal Dalal (Rs 50,000), Thirumuru Maniratnam (Rs 50,000),Ankush (Rs 75,000), Kapil Pokhariya (not covered under TOPS);Neeru Dhanda (Rs 1,00,000),Pincky Balhara (Rs 75,000),Seema (Rs 25,000), Baranica Elangoan and Yashvir Singh (both not covered under TOPS).
Article Summary: Kumkum Mohod became the first Indian woman to win an individual recurve gold at the Games, defeating South Korea’s Oh Yejin 6-5 after a shoot-off. The funding support extended to her puts her targeted assistance at just Rs 50,000. The contrast becomes sharper when placed alongside athletes receiving substantially larger targeted allocations.

NEW DELHI: Lovlina Borgohain ’s Asian Games gold was not just a medal upgrade from silver in the last edition. It was the latest marker in a 15-year career that has taken the Assam boxer through Olympic success, injuries, difficult phases and a mentally demanding Paris 2024 campaign.At the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Borgohain finally changed the colour of her Asian Games medal, defeating China’s Bao Ziyi 5-0 in the women’s 75kg final. The victory, on her 29th birthday, made her only the second Indian woman after MC Mary Kom to win boxing gold at the Asian Games -- 12 years after Kom’s 2014 triumph.For Borgohain, however, the gold's significance went beyond the history books.“It’s still difficult to get out of this moment. I still have the gold medal in my hand," said a beaming Borgohain while lifting the gold medal next to her face. "It’s a very special moment for me. I can’t express how I feel,” she continued as she spoke to TimesofIndia.com upon returning from Japan.Borgohain had finished with silver at the 2022 Hangzhou Asian Games, losing to China’s Li Qian in the final. Three years later, she returned to the continental stage determined to go one step further.Her path to the gold in Nagoya was not straightforward. She began with a 5-0 quarter-final win over South Korea’s Seong Su-yeon before edging Kazakhstan’s reigning 70kg world champion Natalya Bogdanova 3-2 in a closely fought semi-final.She then produced a 5-0 win over Ziyi in the final.The contrast with Hangzhou made the medal particularly meaningful.“Every event is very important. We believe that the Asian Games medal is the highest after the Olympics. I think this medal is shining amidst all the medals. The colour has changed. This medal means a lot to me,” Borgohain said.“I got a silver medal in the last Asian Games and this time I got a gold medal. This is why it is so special. And to do it on my birthday is extra special.”The victory also continued a curious connection between Borgohain and Japan. Five years ago, Tokyo had brought her an Olympic bronze medal — the breakthrough that changed the trajectory of her career.“I was very excited because I was going to Japan again. I had won a medal in (the) 2020 Olympics in Japan, and my life changed because of that,” she said.“I had a positive mindset before leaving India. I wanted to make it the best tournament of my life. I knew that I could do it because Japan is lucky for me.”The gold also offered a reminder of Borgohain’s ability to rebuild.Her career has not followed a straight line since the Tokyo Olympics. Injuries, changes in form and the disappointment of the Paris Olympics tested her, while the pressure that came with becoming an Olympic medallist added another layer to the challenge.Borgohain does not, however, see the Asian Games gold as something that has fundamentally changed her.“I don’t think I am looking at myself differently because of this medal. I have won and lost a lot of medals. People’s perspective changes because of the medal. But I am always the same in my own eyes,” she said.“My perspective has not changed because of the medal. When I lose, my self-belief remains the same. Sometimes I am confident, and sometimes I am down. But I am the same person that I was before.”That mindset became particularly important after Paris 2024, when she failed to reach the medal rounds. Borgohain describes the period as one of the most difficult phases of her career.“I have a 15-year journey. Every time I go to a competition, my mindset is different. When we play, we reach the medal. It is not easy to recover from a tough period. The 2024 Paris Olympics wasn’t an easy period for me mentally,” she said.“But I think everything is a game of the mind. It depends on how we look at it. If we take tough things easy, it becomes easy. If we take easy things hard, it becomes hard. I think that helped me a lot to keep myself calm and relaxed.”The Asian Games victory has also given Borgohain a more direct route towards the next stage of her career. The gold means she qualifies for the World Championships, rather than having to go through the national selection route. A strong performance there could also put her on the road to another Olympic qualification campaign.“It matters a lot for an athlete because of this medal I am qualifying for the World Championships. I am getting a good treat otherwise I would have to play the Nationals and follow the same process,” she said.“So that is a big advantage of the medal, and it boosts my confidence that I can do better. If I do well there, then I can qualify for the Olympics also.”For now, though, Borgohain is resisting the temptation to look too far ahead.“There is a lot of planning. But not everything is the same. I am living in the present. I don’t know what will happen tomorrow. I will try to live like this. It makes me feel good. I will try to live like this.”Borgohain’s gold was part of a strong boxing campaign for India at the Asian Games. India finished the competition with six boxing medals, including three golds, with Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal also winning their respective finals.Some months back, Indian boxers had returned with 10 medals at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, including seven golds. No country had won more golds in boxing at a single edition of the CWG. It was also India's largest haul in the sport in a CWG.For Borgohain, the improvement reflects a broader change in the mentality of Indian boxers.“We had a very good performance. Both men and women did very well. Everyone knows the results of the Commonwealth Games. The results of the Commonwealth Games changed the results of Indian Boxing,” she said.“In the Asian Games, our Indian team came out on top. I think our athletes are very strong. Their mentality is very good. We used to think that we would not be able to do it. But now our young athletes have the mindset that ‘we have to do it’.”She also pointed to the support structure around the team, including government backing and the environment created by the coaching staff led by Santiago Nieva.“The support of the government matters a lot. They don’t let us down. We are getting good competition. The environment of our foreign coaches, led by Santiago (Nieva), is very positive. That is why we are getting good results.”For Borgohain, then, the Asian Games gold is both an ending and a beginning — the end of a 12-year wait since Mary Kom’s historic gold and the completion of a personal journey from Hangzhou silver to Nagoya gold.But she is not treating it as a destination. The next target can wait. For now, she is content to live in the moment — with the gold medal still in her hand.
Article Summary: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain won gold at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya. She beat China's Bao Ziyi 5-0 in the women's 75kg final. The victory, on her 29th birthday, made her only the second Indian woman after Mary Kom to win boxing gold.

Article Title: Vithya Ramraj on newfound fame: 'I'm still far away from reaching world standards'
Article Text:
Vithya Ramraj (Image credit: PTI)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

CHENNAI: With three medals and newfound recognition, Vithya Ramraj returned home from the Asian Games with plenty to celebrate. People at petrol bunks, airports and bus stands have started recognizing her, but it has left the 28-year old, who broke P T Usha’s 400 metre 42-year-old hurdles record, slightly surprised.“People are recognising me now and I’m happy athletics is growing. I’m also thinking about the recognition I am getting. Is it because of the relay medals or because I broke the record? Why have I become famous? That is one constant thing on my mind. I’m still far away from reaching world standards, and my coach was not happy with the timing.“Personally, I didn’t get the satisfaction even though people celebrated. I think of how Neeraj Chopra is celebrated, and if I reach his level, then more people will know me,” Vithya told TOI.What worked for Vithya in 400m hurdles was that she brought down her stride count from 17 to 16 between hurdles 5 and 6.“In the bend from the fifth to the sixth hurdle, I used to take 17 strides, but I have now reduced it to 16. We have been working on it since Nov last year. That helped me going into the home stretch.”Going into the Asian Games, Vithya did not dip below 56 seconds even once this season. While she bagged gold at the Federation Cup and Inter-state athletics meet, her coach Nehpal Singh, who has been a strong source of support, was not satisfied with the medals.“My coach told me, ‘Did I train you to run 56 seconds? What performance have you put in?’”What Vithya felt helped her in the run-up to the Asian Games was the training stints she had in Poland and the Czech Republic with Nehpal.“I used to sleep for 10 hours for three months during the stint abroad, but in India, I used to sleep only for 7-8 hours. In India, I cannot train at 10 am due to the climate, but the sleep cycle in Poland helped me. In India, I train from 5:30am to 8:30am,” she said.
Article Summary: Vithya Ramraj won three medals at the Asian Games. She broke P T Usha’s 400 metre 42-year-old hurdles record. Her coach Nehpal Singh was not satisfied with the medals. Vithya felt training in Poland and the Czech Republic helped her.

NEW DELHI: Two years ago, Sujeet Kalkal was stranded at Dubai International Airport, watching his Olympic dream slip away with every passing hour.On his way to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, for the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament, Kalkal was stuck in Dubai for three days after floods disrupted his travel plans. By the time a flight was arranged, it was too late. He could not reach Bishkek in time, and with it went his chance to qualify for the Paris Olympics.Two years later, the disappointment of Dubai has been replaced by an Asian Games gold. Kalkal, the world No. 2 in the men's 65kg category, fought back from 2-9 down against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev in the final to win 10-9, ending India's eight-year wait for a wrestling gold at the Games.The comeback was symbolic of what Kalkal's career has looked like since that Olympic setback. He has had to rebuild, compete through the disappointment and find a way back to the biggest stages. On Sunday, he did that with an Asian Games title.When the final whistle came, Kalkal folded his hands, looked up and thanked God. He then took a lap of the arena with the Indian tricolour draped around his shoulders, tears and a broad smile.For a wrestler who had once been denied even the chance to fight for an Olympic place, the moment carried a little more weight than an Asian Games gold."This gold means a lot to me. Not just because it is an Asian Games gold, but because there is so much behind this medal. The last few years have had many ups and downs, and I missed a few opportunities, but I never lost belief in myself," Kalkal told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview on his way back to Imlota village in Bhiwani, Haryana, where his parents were waiting to welcome him.The Dubai episode, he says, is now behind him. What remains is the lesson from it - and a much bigger target."Paris was very difficult for me to miss, but that experience made me stronger instead of breaking me. LA 2028 is obviously a very big goal for me," Kalkal said.And he is clear about what he wants from that opportunity. "Olympics mein jaana hai toh sirf participate karne ke liye nahi jaana, bhaisaab. Gold ke liye jaana hai [“If you’re going to the Olympics, don’t go just to participate, brother. Go there to win gold]."India had not won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games since 2018. Kalkal's victory ended that wait and added another major title to a career that already includes an U23 World Championship crown, Asian Championships success and a Zagreb Open triumph."India has won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games after eight years, so being a part of it is very special for me. This medal reminds me that if you keep working hard, your time will come," he said.The road to the Asian Games gold was not easy for Kalkal. He had a challenging draw, but handled each bout with confidence.After a comfortable opening victory, he made a statement in the quarterfinals by throwing Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi from a standing position within the opening 20 seconds.The semifinal brought an even bigger test, but Kalkal overcame Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka to reach the gold medal bout.Then came the final against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev, and it looked like the toughest challenge of them all.Instead of allowing the deficit to affect him, Kalkal fought his way back into the contest. He produced eight points to turn a seven-point deficit into a 10-9 victory and seal the Asian Games title."The simple plan was to wrestle my own way and not be impressed by my opponent's name. Whether he is an Olympic champion, a world champion or anyone else, everyone starts from zero on the mat. I just trusted my preparation and my strength. I knew that if I executed my best, I could beat anyone. Instead of thinking too much during the match, I just had to fight for every single point," he said.Kalkal also dedicated the gold to the country and remembered his father, who stood by him throughout his journey."I dedicate this gold to the whole of India. Of course, my first call was to my father. He has supported me tremendously throughout this journey, and without his support, it would have been impossible for me to reach this point. His support will always remain with me," the Indian wrestler said.The final also reflected the mental change Kalkal says came from the disappointment of 2024."Fear may never completely go away, but now I know how to fight with fear. When you go through tough situations in life, small things stop bothering you. What happened in Dubai, missing the Olympic qualifiers - every experience taught me something," the Indian wrestler said."Now I don't run away from pressure. I enjoy pressure because those are the moments when you realise how strong you actually are," Kalkal said.The Asian Games gold now joins an already impressive list of achievements for Kalkal, but he is not dwelling on the medals he has already won. The next target is Los Angeles. And this time, he wants to get there on his own terms."Gold ke liye jaana hai."
Article Summary: Two years ago, Sujeet Kalkal was stranded at Dubai International Airport. He was on his way to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, for the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament. Two years later, the disappointment of Dubai has been replaced by an Asian Games gold. He fought back from 2-9 down against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev.

Article Title: Other side of India's Asian Games success: 201 athletes won just 6 bronze, 137 returned empty-handed
Article Text:
AP Photo

The spending breakdown
